### Tone, syllables and stress

No phonemic tone.
Syllable shapes (share of syllables in the word-shape model): CV 85%, V 15%. At most 1 consonant(s) before the vowel and 0 after it.
No fixed stress position: prominence is not tied to a syllable, so no stress mark is written (as in French phrases, Korean or many Austronesian languages; the engine has no word-by-word lexical stress yet).
Core words average 2.77 syllables (5.1 sounds); 26% of words share their form with another word.

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). Allophones are spelled as their phonemes.

**Consonants:** m ‹m› · n ‹n› · b ‹b› · d ‹d› · ᵐb ‹mb› · ⁿd ‹nd› · ᵑɡ ‹ngg› · ⁿdz ‹ndz› · s ‹s› · ʁ ‹ġ› · h ‹h› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · l ‹l›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · u ‹u› · a ‹a›

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is VOS; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessed before the possessor; noun before the adjective; noun before the demonstrative; numeral order varies; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-initial.
It has a definite article after the noun, an indefinite article, a rich case system, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), singular and plural, no gender or noun classes.
Verbs mark past, future, perfective and habitual; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator after the verb; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs agree with the subject by suffixes; not with the object.
Other features: serial verbs; verb reduplication; a copula; adjectives that behave like verbs; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words moved to the front; a decimal counting base; a 'have' verb for possession.
Measured morphology: 17 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.5 (0 free word … 3 fused), 60 paradigm cells, 19 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns mark number: plural: a suffix (la, from 'many').

| *ahai* |
| --- |
| dog |

‘dog’

| *ahai-la* |
| --- |
| dog-PL |

‘dogs’

**Case.** Nouns take 3 case markers: genitive (GEN): a clitic after the noun phrase (iᵐbi; jiᵐbi after a front or central vowel; from 'that'); locative (LOC): a clitic after the noun phrase (nuᵑɡa, from 'head'); comitative (COM): a clitic after the noun phrase (ᵑɡulu, from 'with'). Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them.

| *umi=jiᵐbi* |
| --- |
| man=GEN |

‘of the man’

| *lahuhuhi=nuᵑɡa* |
| --- |
| house=LOC |

‘in the house’

| *ahai=ᵑɡulu* |
| --- |
| dog=COM |

‘with the dog’

**Gender and noun classes.** There is no gender or noun class.

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Past (PST): a prefix (ᵑɡu; ᵑɡuw in some words (sound change at the join); from 'yesterday'); perfect (PRF): a prefix (mi; mij in some words (sound change at the join); from 'hold'); future (FUT): a prefix (a, from 'go'); habitual (HAB): a clitic before the verb (ai, from 'do'); inceptive ('begin to') (INCH): a prefix (a, from 'begin'). Unmarked: progressive (left to context).

| *ᵑɡuw-aⁿdi* |
| --- |
| PST-go |

‘(it) went’

| *mij-aⁿdi* |
| --- |
| PRF-go |

‘(it) has gone’

| *a-jaⁿdi* |
| --- |
| FUT-go |

‘(it) will go’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 2SG: a suffix (ma, from 'thou'); 3PL: a suffix (li, from 'they'). No marker yet for 1SG, 3SG, 1PL, 2PL (zero).

| *aⁿdi-ma* |
| --- |
| go-2SG |

‘you go’

| *aⁿdi-li* |
| --- |
| go-3PL |

‘they go’

**Negation.** Negation is a suffix (ᵐbi, from 'nothing').

| *ihi-ᵐbi* | *hiju=wiᵐbi* | *imimi* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| drink-NEG | milk=DEF | 1SG |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a particle at the end of the clause. Question words move to the front: who ilihi, what mila, where ihi, when ᵑɡami, how mili.

| *uluhuwi-ma=ᵑɡaᵐbi* | *ihumuⁿdu=wiᵐbi* | *ma* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| hear-2SG=Q | thunder=DEF | 2SG |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *mila* | *lihiju* | *liᵑɡu=wiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what | bring | child=DEF |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *ihiba* | *du=wiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- |
| eat | fish=DEF |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands after the possessed noun, marked by the genitive marker, a clitic after the noun phrase (iᵐbi). 'Having' is said with a 'have' verb ('my mother has a boat').

| *ahai* | *umi=jiᵐbi=jiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | man=DEF=GEN |

‘the man's dog’

| *aunaju* | *bibu=lahuhuhihi* | *uhala* | *imimi=jiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| have | INDF=boat | mother | 1SG=GEN |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *duʁuᵑɡu=wiᵐbi* | *iᵐbihilama* | *babi* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| woman=DEF | REL | dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is a prefix (li, from 'he'). Adjectives behave like verbs: 'the water is cold' is said as 'the water colds', with the verb's markers.

| *umi* | *iᵐbihilama* | *bibu=li-jibu* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| man | that | INDF=COP-merchant |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *binubu* | *ilimubi=jiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- |
| cold | water=DEF |

‘the water is cold’

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action done intensely (INTS), by copying the whole stem.

| *aⁿdi-aⁿdi* |
| --- |
| INTS-go |

‘(an action done intensely)’

| *ihiba-ihiba* | *du=wiᵐbi* | *umi=jiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| INTS-eat | fish=DEF | man=DEF |

‘The man really eats the fish.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Serial verbs.** Verbs can be strung together in one clause with one subject (serial verbs): 'take X come' is 'bring'. 'Go' after a motion verb gives its direction ('run go' = run away).

| *alihina* | *du=wiᵐbi* | *lihihi* | *umi=jiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| take | fish=DEF | come | man=DEF |

‘The man brings the fish (takes it and comes).’ (sentence 13 below)

| *aⁿdaᵐbimu* | *aⁿdi* |
| --- | --- |
| run | go |

‘run away’

**Giving (two objects).** No dative: a serial construction, 'take the thing, give (it to) the person'.

| *alihina* | *du=wiᵐbi* | *maᵑɡi* | *liᵑɡu=wiᵐbi* | *duʁuᵑɡu=wiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| take | fish=DEF | give | child=DEF | woman=DEF |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is ihamumu and a hundred is hilau.

| *hamumubibu* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *hamumumihi* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *lihahamumu* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *lubaⁿduhu* | *du* | *ahai=jiᵐbi* | *umi=jiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| say | sleep | dog=DEF | man=DEF |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Word shapes.** Some markers sound the same: DEF and GEN are both iᵐbi; FUT and INCH are both a; 3PL and COP are both li (context tells them apart).

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' luᵑɡanuluᵑɡahu (near) and 'that' iᵐbihilama (far).

| *ahai* | *luᵑɡanuluᵑɡahu* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | this |

‘this dog’

| *ahai* | *iᵐbihilama* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | that |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** An 'exceed' comparison: 'A is big, exceeds B', with the verb for 'climb' (as Yoruba ju 'exceed', Thai kwaa 'cross over').

| *umi=jiᵐbi* | *liⁿdaⁿdi* | *anu* | *ahai=jiᵐbi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man=DEF | big | exceed | dog=DEF |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 17 below)

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 4 families of 3+ words; 14% of the 759 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **brother** *lirimiri* (N, coined 11.5 kyr ago in cloud giant 1); 4 words have it as their main root, 4 contain it.

| meaning | IPA | spelling | roots (main first) | how it was built |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| brother | lihimihi | lihimihi | brother | \*nuttimiti 'sibling' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → 'sibling' > 'brother' (11.5) |
| mother's brother | lihimijuhala | lihimiyuhala | brother, mother | \*nuttimiti 'sibling' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → 'sibling' > 'brother' (11.5) → BROTHER + MOTHER = 'mother's brother' (0.5) |
| parallel cousin | lihimihi | lihimihi | brother | \*nuttimiti 'sibling' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → 'sibling' > 'brother' (11.5) → colex:BROTHER (11.5) |
| younger brother | lihimihiliᵑɡuwi | lihimihilingguwi | brother, child (young human) | \*nuttimiti 'sibling' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → 'sibling' > 'brother' (11.5) → BROTHER + SMALL = 'younger brother' (0) |

### Families a historian reconstructs

The roots a historian reconstructs: every word's family as it was when the word was made, carried forward however opaque it has become since (per-word `etym_roots`, the *bher- 'carry' > burden view). 53 families of 3+ words; 51% of the 759 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **see** *lidatwaw* (V, coined 20 kyr ago in the cloud giant proto-language); 8 words have it as their main root, 8 contain it.

| meaning | IPA | spelling | roots (main first) | how it was built |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cheek | lihabi | lihabi | see | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → SEE + 'thing' = 'face' (5) → 'face' > 'cheek' (1.5) |
| eye | lihai | lihai | see | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → SEE + 'thing' = 'eye' (3.5) |
| face | lihabi | lihabi | see | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → SEE + 'thing' = 'face' (5) |
| forehead | lihabainuᵑɡaⁿda | lihabainungganda | see, head | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → SEE + 'thing' = 'face' (5) → FACE + HEAD = 'forehead' (4.5) |
| look | lihaba | lihaba | see | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → 'see' > 'look' (4) |
| navel | lihaibu | lihaibu | see, belly | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → SEE + 'thing' = 'eye' (3.5) → EYE + BELLY = 'navel' (1) |
| see | lihaba | lihaba | see | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) |
| show | lihabumu | lihabumu | see | \*lidatwaw 'see' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → SEE + 'cause' = 'show' (6.5) → SHOW + 'intens' = 'show' (0.5) |

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are a short sentence about the birth run together (as Yoruba *Babatunde* 'father has returned'); the byname is an epithet after the name. The tradition goes back to the cloud giant proto-language.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |
\|---\|---\|---\|---\|---\|
| **Minggabiba** | /miᵑɡabiba/ | 'father has returned' | old | Minggabiba 'father has returned': minggabi 'return home' + ba 'father'; an old name, coined in d131 4.0 kyr ago as Minggabiba |
| **Minggabihinggili** | /miᵑɡabihiᵑɡili/ | 'the spirit has come home' | old | Minggabihinggili 'the spirit has come home': minggabi 'return home' + singgili 'spirit'; an old name, coined in d131 4.0 kyr ago as Minggabisinggili |
| **Hiu** | /hiu/ | 'God knows' | old, opaque | Hiu 'God knows': hiyunu 'know' + ilana 'god'; an old name, coined in d131 4.0 kyr ago as Hiyunuilana, worn down in use |
| **Hiyunuilana** | /hijunuilana/ | 'God knows' | new | Hiyunuilana 'God knows': hiyunu 'know' + ilana 'god'; coined from today's words |
| **Lihihilinggu** | /lihihiliᵑɡu/ | 'the child came' | new | Lihihilinggu 'the child came': lihihi 'come' + linggu 'child'; coined from today's words |
| **Milihauhala** | /milihauhala/ | 'mother laughed' | new | Milihauhala 'mother laughed': milihambihi 'laugh' + uhala 'mother'; coined from today's words |
| **Minggabiba Bi** | /miᵑɡabiba bi/ | 'father has returned, the white' | epithet | bi 'white', a byname |
| **Minggabihinggili Ngginggu** | /miᵑɡabihiᵑɡili ᵑɡiᵑɡu/ | 'the spirit has come home, the strong' | epithet | ngginggu 'strong', a byname |

**Settlements.** **Ihilibi** /ihilibi/ (town, 8,540): 'the low market'; named by the kobold (d440) who founded it 5.0 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Ililabilu** /ililabilu/ (town, 8,154): 'the small market'; named by the kobold (d440) who founded it 1.2 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Lahili** /lahili/ (town, 7,579): 'the old fence'; named by the kobold (d440) who founded it 5.0 kyr ago, kept as heard.

## Gods and liturgy

**Faith.** The mountain faith of the earliest cloud giants of the west of Simath, founded 300 kyr ago ago, held by 11 languages.

| god | name | IPA | meaning | the same name elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| god of mountain and forest | **Ubamana** | /ubamana/ | 'mountain-grandfather' | — |
| god of sky and storm | **Nggabiyuhi** | /ᵑɡabijuhi/ | 'lord of the sky' | — |
| god of hunt and fertility | **Ihanggubi** | /ihaᵑɡubi/ | 'the hunter' | — |
| god of hearth and smithing | **Ubaluhu** | /ubaluhu/ | 'the one who burns' | — |

How the first name came about: 'mountain-grandfather' (a kin title) in p103, 20 kyr ago.

**Liturgy.** The faith's rites are kept in the cloud giant speech of cloud giant 1 as it was 6.5 kyr ago ago, frozen since (as Latin, Sanskrit or Ge'ez are).

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
